And when reading four for the last, the last's superiority is also known to all, as Magen Avraham wrote afterward; therefore no honor and no embarrassment for the oleh, as above. The Rabbi did not see in Yerushalmi end that if one skipped one verse on Shabbat he returns, opens, blesses, and reads — see there; but on additional festival portions there is room to question. Since Turei Zahav wrote anonymously it implies no distinction — as if he only saw Beit Yosef and not the body of the law in Turei Zahav that deals with what is written in several places about Shirat HaYam and the Ten Commandments with the shatz when they do not hear from the shatz, etc., and discussed this; and on this he wrote but on seven days of Pesach and Shavuot there is not such stringency since they already read the portions on their Shabbats — like Monday and Thursday; if so Turei Zahav did not come to teach the law of festivals but incidentally, and we find nothing to infer from his anonymity. Tosafot Megillah 23 wrote: if on Yom Tov one read the whole minyan and forgot to read the day's obligation, he returns to the scroll and another reads the day's obligation, and the last who read before is as if he does not exist. It appears to me that since he wrote anonymously he holds on all festivals one returns — not only on the festival where the Gemara's law is to read festival offerings, but even on other festivals where R' Akiva's enactment is to read the day's offerings as Tosafot and Rosh wrote there, and so Beit Yosef siman 282 in the name of Shlah — still they must be read, for what harm if read immediately or later — it does not cause another blessing; but if one skipped one verse he does not return, for he is no worse than the festival portion itself mentioned in the Gemara which nevertheless does not require return — all the more so additional offerings. And now in our case where he skipped, on day 3 it is as if he did not read at all, lest today be day 3; especially for us who are expert in calendar fixation that it is certain. And what he wrote that because of doubt we do not bless — requires further study, for every second day of Yom Tov is doubtful and we bless on kiddush and havdalah many blessings since the Sages enacted — see Tosafot Sukkah 44 and Shabbat 23. Also some proof from Keriat Shema above siman 64 seif 2, that the law of skipping one word is like skipping an entire verse, as Levush wrote; and although in Tur and Shulchan Aruch there only an entire verse is mentioned, perforce one must say one word is the same, as Tosafot and Rosh wrote in Berachot 15a. Also it appears to me to learn from there: if he skipped a word he need not return and read from the start of the verse but from that word, as Levush wrote there and Lechem Chamudot 14a, until here; and the same applies when an error is found in a Torah scroll; see Beit Yosef siman 104; and so the wording implies in siman 143 seif 4: they begin from the place where the error was found, etc.

And they brought in Shakhnei HaGedolah in Hagahot Tashbetz note 1, Orach Torah note 3; and Peri Chadash agreed note 2; and so is Yeshuot Yaakov's view. And so appears from Mechaber's words that there is no difference whether he reads himself or the chazzan reads for him; see Sefer A"R note 1 who wrote another explanation: l'chatchila call for one, and if not for two, etc., see there. We have only Mechaber's words and his view: whichever one the chazzan wishes, call him for four, and there is no stringency; and so is the practice.

eliyah_rabbah.en: [5] He returns and reads, etc. — with two verses with him, etc. — so Beit Yosef wrote in the name of Hagahot Maimoniyot. And Maharam of Lublin wrote in responsum siman 88, and this is his language: since it is not explained in Hagahot Maimoniyot that he returns and blesses, it could be he returns and reads without a blessing — and so the wording implies, until here his language. Sheyarei Knesset HaGedolah and Olat Tamid brought this to decide halachah; but Sheyarei Knesset HaGedolah wrote: I do not know what is different about Parashat Parah at the end of this siman, until here. And in Olat Tamid he forced a distinction; and in Eliyahu Zuta I wondered that it escaped all the great ones mentioned above — Massekhet Soferim chapter 21 halachah 4, this is its language: he returns, opens, blesses, and reads — he and two others, until here — behold it is explicit that he blesses. And it is more astonishing that they only saw Beit Yosef and did not examine Hagahot Maimoniyot itself, which wrote explicitly chapter 12 of Laws of Prayer that he blesses, and Beit Yosef copied briefly. And it appears to me he truly relied on Parashat Parah at the end of this siman that one blesses; and now what Sheyarei Knesset HaGedolah wondered in note 1 — this is its language: wonder on Hagahot Maimoniyot, from where that he reads with two others? In Massekhet Soferim this is not mentioned, until here his language — meaning he also only saw chapter 1 of Massekhet Soferim and not chapter 21, where it teaches explicitly with two others; and this is a novel matter on a great collection like him. Also what Olat Tamid left in "requires study for practice" regarding skipping three verses and whether one blesses — see there; he is certainly mistaken, for even for one verse one blesses; and it is obvious that even if seven men read and each three verses without the skipped verse, he returns and reads.
